title: Stubborn Visionaries & Pigheaded Fools: how to decide when to persist or quit
summary: Jason Cohen argues that success-through-perseverance and failure-through-obstinance look identical at the moment of decision, so nobody can know in advance which one they're in. The job is to decide decisively, measure honestly, and use practical questions (timeboxes, existence proofs, sounding boards) to find out fast.

principles.text: At the decision point, persevering and obstinate paths are indistinguishable; you can't know which one you're on.
principles.quote: Consider S1 and S2 at time (B). Up to this point they are identical.

principles.text: Even experts and professional investors can't tell which path you're on, so don't expect certainty before deciding.
principles.quote: Not even the experts know which path you're on.

principles.text: Stopping guarantees failure while persisting at least leaves success possible, so quitting early has a real cost.
principles.quote: Stopping means you'll never create something great.

principles.text: Hindsight stories about perseverance or obstinacy are rationalizations; judging decisions by outcomes teaches less than we think.
principles.quote: The typical, backward-looking interpretation of these two scenarios is not the best way for us to understand the choices in front of us today

principles.text: Accepting uncertainty frees you to decide quickly, with less second-guessing and less guilt or cockiness afterward.
principles.quote: it liberates you to make decisions more easily--with less second-guessing in the moment, and less guilt afterwards.

principles.text: Use a hard timebox, and an existence proof from others who succeeded, as practical tests for whether to keep going.
principles.quote: Set a hard deadline for how much longer you'll work on it without seeing improvement.
